title: Institutions Rule: The Primacy of Institutions over Geography and Integration in Economic Development
research_question: What are the relative contributions of the quality of domestic institutions (property rights and rule of law), international trade integration, and geography in determining cross-country differences in long-run income per capita? Once these deep determinants are considered jointly, which factor exerts the dominant direct effect on income levels, and how do these factors influence one another?
data_description: The analysis uses cross-country data on 64, 80, and 140 countries (the latter two being the main samples). The dependent variable is log GDP per capita on a PPP basis in 1995 from the Penn World Tables. Institutional quality is measured by the Kaufmann-Kraay-Zoido-Lobaton rule-of-law index (ranging from -2.5 to 2.5). Integration is measured as the ratio of nominal trade (imports plus exports) to GDP, averaged over 1950-98. Geography is proxied by absolute distance from the equator, with alternative measures including tropical land share, frost days/area, malaria prevalence, mean temperature, and access to sea. Additional variables include log European settler mortality, predicted trade shares from a gravity equation (Frankel-Romer), fractions of the population speaking English and other European languages, legal origin, colonizer identity, religion, and regional dummies. Auxiliary regressions use income, capital, human capital per worker, and TFP from Hall and Jones.
institutional_context: The motivating setting is the enormous variation in income levels across countries—per capita GDP differs by a factor of more than 100 between the richest and poorest nations. Three competing intellectual traditions seek to explain this: a geography-based view (climate, disease burden, agricultural productivity, transport costs) associated with Diamond and Sachs; an integration view emphasizing international trade and market access associated with Frankel-Romer and earlier Sachs-Warner work; and an institutions view emphasizing property rights and rule of law associated with North and with Acemoglu-Johnson-Robinson. The colonial experience of European powers provides historical variation: in regions where European settlers faced low mortality, colonizers established institutions protecting property rights, whereas in high-mortality regions they built extractive institutions. Linguistic legacies (fractions speaking English or other European languages) also reflect colonial influence. These historical patterns create plausibly exogenous variation in current institutional quality and openness.
